chapters.name: Chapter 1: Your first lines of code

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What code is, and where AI fits in
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain what a program is and how an AI assistant can help you learn to code.
This lesson builds toward: In your own words, you will explain what code and a program are, and how to use AI as a tutor instead of a ghostwriter within your school's rules, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
Code is a list of instructions a computer follows exactly, in order. A program is a set of those instructions that does a job, like a game, an app or a calculator. Python is a popular coding language because its words look a lot like English.
AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini can write and explain code. That is useful, but if you copy code you do not understand, you learn nothing and you cannot fix it when it breaks. In this course, AI is your tutor, not your ghostwriter.
Schools have different rules about AI. Some classes allow it for practice but not for graded work. Always check your teacher's rules, and say when you used AI. Many AI tools also have a minimum age, so read the tool's terms and ask a parent or guardian before you sign up.
Words to know:
- Code: instructions written for a computer to follow.
- Program: a set of instructions that does a job.
- Python: a popular coding language that is easy to read.
Try it now: Write down one small program you would like to build someday, like a quiz about your favorite game or a tip calculator for your first job. Then write one sentence on how AI could help you learn it without doing it for you.
You can now say what code and a program are, and explain how to use AI as a tutor instead of a shortcut.

check.q: Why is Python a popular first coding language?
options: Its words look a lot like English
check.why: Python's words look a lot like English, which makes it easier to read.

check.q: A friend says, "Just have AI write your whole program and hand it in." What do you say?
options: I will use AI as a tutor and write the code myself, following my teacher's rules
Good idea; no one will know
I will copy it but change the names
check.why: Copying code you do not understand teaches nothing and may break school rules.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Running your first Python code in Google Colab
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Open a free Colab notebook and run a line of Python.
This lesson builds toward: Using a Google account you are allowed to use, you will open a Google Colab notebook and run Python code that prints text, without help, with the output showing under the cell.
Google Colab is a free notebook that runs Python in your web browser. You do not need to install anything. You need a Google account. Check its age rules, and if you are under 18 ask a parent or guardian first; a school Google account may work if your school allows Colab.
A notebook is made of cells. A code cell is a box where you type Python. You press the play button next to the cell (or Shift and Enter) to run it, and the result shows underneath.
The first command most coders learn is print. It shows words on the screen. Text goes inside quotes, like this: print("Hello, I am learning Python").
Step by step:
- Open a web browser and go to colab.research.google.com.
- Sign in with a Google account you are allowed to use.
- Create a new notebook.
- Click in the first code cell and type: print("Hello, I am learning Python")
- Press the play button or Shift and Enter. Read the output under the cell.
Words to know:
- Notebook: a page where you write and run code in small boxes called cells.
- Cell: one box in a notebook where you type code.
- Output: what the program shows after it runs.
Try it now: In a new Colab notebook, print three lines: your first name, your favorite song or game, and one goal for this course. Run the cell and check all three lines appear.
You can now open a Colab notebook, type Python in a cell, run it, and read the output.

check.q: In Python, what does print do?
options: Sends your code to a printer
Shows words or values on the screen
check.why: print shows text or values under the cell when it runs.

check.q: You are 14 and want to use Colab at home. What do you do first?
options: Make an account with a fake age
Check the age rules and ask a parent or guardian, or use an allowed school account
check.why: Colab needs a Google account; check its rules and involve a parent or guardian if you are under 18.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Variables, input, if and loops
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use a variable, ask for input, make a decision with if, and repeat with a loop.
This lesson builds toward: Given a one-question quiz to build, you will write Python that uses a variable, input, if and else, and a loop, so it runs correctly with both a right and a wrong answer.
A variable is a named box that stores a value. score = 0 makes a box called score and puts 0 in it. Later, score = score + 1 adds one point.
input asks the player to type something: name = input("What is your name? "). An if statement makes a decision: if answer == "Paris": print("Correct!") else: print("Not quite"). Two equals signs mean "is the same as". The lines under if and else are pushed in with spaces; this is called indentation, and Python needs it.
A loop repeats code. for i in range(3): print("Go team!") prints the cheer three times. These four ideas, variables, input, if and loops, are enough to build a quiz game.
Step by step:
- Make a variable: score = 0
- Ask for input: name = input("What is your name? ")
- Make a decision with if and else, indenting the lines under each.
- Repeat something with: for i in range(3):
Words to know:
- Variable: a named box that stores a value.
- Input: something the user types in while the program runs.
- If statement: code that runs only when something is true.
- Loop: code that repeats.
- Indentation: spaces at the start of a line that show which lines belong together.
Try it now: Write a one-question quiz: ask for the player's name, ask one question about your favorite subject or game, and use if and else to print "Correct" or "Not quite". Run it twice, once with the right answer and once with a wrong one.
You can now use a variable, input, an if statement and a loop in a small Python program.

options: The spaces that push lines in under an if, else or loop
check.why: Indentation shows which lines belong under an if, else or loop, and Python needs it.

check.q: You want the quiz to add a point for a right answer. Which line do you write under the if?
check.why: score = score + 1 adds one point to the value stored in score.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Coding with an AI helper

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Asking AI to explain code
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask an AI assistant to explain a piece of code line by line, and check you understand it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a few lines of code, you will ask an AI assistant to explain the code line by line, then change one thing, predict the result and run it, pasting no private information.
Paste a few lines of code into an AI assistant and ask: "Explain this Python code line by line for a beginner. Use simple words." A good explanation tells you what each line does and why.
Then test your understanding. Change one thing in the code, guess what will happen, and run it. If your guess was right, you understand it. If not, ask the AI: "I changed this and expected that. Why did it do something else?"
Do not paste private information into an AI tool: no passwords, home address, school ID numbers or phone numbers. Code for a class project does not need any of them.
Step by step:
- Copy 3 to 10 lines of code.
- Ask: "Explain this Python code line by line for a beginner."
- Change one thing and guess what will happen.
- Run it and compare. Ask a follow-up if your guess was wrong.
Words to know:
- Explain line by line: go through code one line at a time and say what each does.
Try it now: Paste your one-question quiz from Lesson 3 into an AI assistant and ask it to explain each line. Then change the right answer to a new one, guess what will happen, and run it.
You can now get a clear line-by-line explanation of code from AI and test that you really understand it.

check.q: What makes a good AI explanation of code?
options: It is as long as possible
It tells what each line does and why
check.why: A good explanation says what each line does and why, in simple words.

check.q: You changed a line, guessed the result, and the program did something else. What next?
options: Ask the AI: "I changed this and expected that. Why did it do something else?"
Paste your password so the AI can check
check.why: A follow-up explaining what you expected helps you understand the code.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Finding and fixing errors with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Read an error message and use AI to help fix a bug.
This lesson builds toward: Given a Python error message, you will find the problem line, fix the bug with AI's help if needed, and run the fix yourself, until the program runs without errors.
A bug is a mistake in code. When Python cannot run a line, it shows an error message. The last line of the message usually names the problem, such as SyntaxError (something is typed wrong) or IndentationError (the spaces at the start of a line are wrong). It also shows the line number.
First try yourself: look at that line for a missing quote, bracket, colon or space. If you are stuck, paste the code and the full error into an AI assistant and ask: "What does this error mean, and how do I fix it? Explain why."
AI can be wrong about code too. Run the fixed version yourself. If the error changes or stays, tell the AI exactly what happened.
Step by step:
- Read the last line of the error message and the line number.
- Check that line for missing quotes, brackets, colons or spaces.
- If stuck, paste the code and the full error into an AI assistant.
- Ask what it means and why the fix works.
- Run the fix yourself and check it works.
Words to know:
- Bug: a mistake in code.
- Error message: Python's note saying what went wrong and on which line.
- Debugging: finding and fixing bugs.
Try it now: In your quiz, delete the colon after the if line on purpose and run it. Read the error. Ask an AI assistant to explain it, fix it, and run the program again.
You can now read a Python error message, look for the problem, and use AI to understand and fix a bug.

check.q: What does a SyntaxError usually mean?
options: Something is typed wrong, like a missing quote or colon
check.why: A SyntaxError means Python cannot read something you typed.

check.q: Python shows an error on line 4. What do you check first?
options: Line 4, for a missing quote, bracket, colon or space
check.why: The message shows the line number; check that line yourself first.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Building your quiz game
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan and build a 5-question quiz game with AI as a helper.
This lesson builds toward: Starting from a plan written as comments, you will build a 5-question quiz game one piece at a time and say how you used AI, with the player's name, score, final message and a comment above each part in your own words.
Big programs are built from small pieces. Plan first: what the program says first, what it asks, how it keeps score, and what it says at the end. Write the plan as short comments. A comment starts with # and Python ignores it.
Build one piece at a time and run it after each piece. If you want an idea, ask AI: "How could I make my quiz tell the player their score out of 5?" Then write it yourself and ask the AI to check it.
When it works, have a friend or family member play it. Watch where they get confused, and improve it. If you turn it in for school, say how you used AI.
Step by step:
- Write a plan as # comments: welcome, questions, score, ending.
- Code the welcome and ask the player's name. Run it.
- Add one question with if and else that changes the score. Run it.
- Add four more questions. Run it.
- Print the final score and a message. Let someone play it.
Words to know:
- Comment: a note in code that starts with # and is ignored by Python.
- Plan: a short list of what your program will do, in order.
Try it now: Final task: build a Python quiz game in Colab with at least 5 questions about a topic you like. Ask the player's name, keep score, print a final message, use AI to explain or fix one part, and write a comment above each part in your own words.
You can now plan, build, test and explain a small Python program, using AI as a helper and not a replacement.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Program runs The program does not run in Colab, or stops with an error. The program runs from start to finish in Colab. It also handles a player typing an answer in a different way, such as capital letters. Building blocks Missing input, if and else, or a score variable. Asks the player's name, uses if and else for at least 5 questions, and keeps score in a variable. Also uses a loop to repeat part of the game. Built in pieces No plan or final message. A plan in comments, five questions and a final message with the score. A friend played it, and the learner improved one part based on what they saw. AI as a tutor AI wrote the program, or AI use is not stated. AI explained or helped fix at least one part, and the learner says how it was used. The learner can show a change they predicted and tested after the AI explanation. Comments in own words Comments are missing or copied from AI. A comment above each part says in the learner's own words what it does. Also notes one bug they fixed and how. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is a comment in Python?
options: A line starting with # that Python ignores
check.why: Comments start with # and are notes for people, not instructions for Python.

check.q: You finished the quiz game. What is a good next step?
options: Ask AI to rewrite it all
Have a friend play it and watch where they get confused
check.why: Watching someone play shows you what to improve.
